criteria.descriptor: Correctly explains why in-place overwrite and Git/Git-LFS fail for large data, and accurately describes immutable/content-addressed versioning, run-to-data pinning, and lineage tooling. Full marks require no technical errors (e.g. correctly stating that snapshot expiry/VACUUM can delete needed versions, that lineage should be machine-captured, and that a stable id links artifact to data).

Covers the full arc: diagnosis, an immutable versioning layer, pinning the run to its exact data/code, transformation lineage, a two-tool comparison with a choice, and the reproduction procedure. Deduct for missing lineage, missing run-to-data pinning, or ignoring retention.

Justifies the chosen versioning approach against at least one alternative with concrete trade-offs tied to this scenario (existing S3/Parquet, audit window, team scale, engine-agnosticism), rather than naming a tool with no rationale.
Reads as a coherent design-review write-up: correct vocabulary (immutable snapshots, content hashing, commit/snapshot ids, lineage DAG), clear structure, and an unambiguous recommendation.

expected_answer_points: Diagnoses the root cause: overwriting 'latest/' in place destroys history, so the model artifact has no immutable pointer to the exact data it trained on (code is versioned in Git, data is not)
Notes plain Git / Git-LFS is unsuitable for large columnar/Parquet datasets and does not capture transformation lineage
Introduces an immutable, versioned/content-addressed data layer giving each dataset state a stable id (e.g. DVC hash, lakeFS commit/tag, or Iceberg/Delta snapshot)
Pins each training run to its inputs by logging dataset version id + code commit SHA + hyperparameters + env/seeds against the model artifact (e.g. via MLflow), and stops overwriting the model file
Captures transformation lineage (OpenLineage/Marquez, dbt, or a catalog), ideally column-level, tracing each feature back to raw source tables
Compares at least two concrete versioning approaches (e.g. DVC vs lakeFS vs Delta/Iceberg time travel) with real trade-offs and justifies a choice for the S3/Parquet context
Describes reproduction: check out pinned commit, resolve pinned data version, restore environment/seeds, re-run
Addresses retention/governance: prevent premature VACUUM / snapshot expiry / S3 lifecycle deletion so the audited version survives the compliance window
common_pitfalls: Proposing to 'just commit the Parquet to Git' or Git-LFS as the whole solution, ignoring that Git chokes on multi-GB columnar data and still provides no run-to-data pinning or lineage
Conflating reproducing the model (code + seed) with reproducing the data - versioning the code but leaving the dataset overwritten in place
Treating time travel as free forever and forgetting Delta VACUUM / Iceberg snapshot expiration / S3 lifecycle rules can delete the exact version the auditor needs
Describing lineage as a hand-drawn diagram or wiki page rather than machine-captured metadata linking artifact to data version to transformation DAG
Only versioning the final training table, not the raw-to-feature transformation graph, so you still can't say which source column produced a value
Naming a tool (DVC/lakeFS/Delta) with no justification or trade-off tied to the team's S3/Parquet setup and audit requirements
reference_answer:
Root cause: the dataset is mutated in place. Git version-controls the code, but the model artifact has no durable pointer to the exact bytes it trained on, and 'latest/' overwrites destroy every prior state. Plain Git and Git-LFS can't efficiently version multi-GB Parquet, nor express which upstream tables produced it. So neither the exact inputs nor the transformation history survive.

Design:
1) Store training data in an immutable, versioned layer so each dataset state gets a stable id (content hash / commit / snapshot). Candidates: DVC (content-hashes the data, commits a small pointer file into Git, pushes blobs to S3); lakeFS (git-style branches/commits/tags over the same S3 buckets with zero-copy branching); or an Iceberg/Delta table with ACID snapshots and time travel.
2) Pin data to each run. In an experiment tracker (e.g. MLflow) log the dataset version id, code commit SHA, hyperparameters, library versions and random seeds against the model artifact, making artifact <-> data <-> code a resolvable triple. Stop overwriting prod.pkl; store versioned artifacts.
3) Capture transformation lineage. Emit lineage from the pipeline (OpenLineage -> Marquez, dbt, or a data catalog), ideally column-level, so each feature traces back to its raw source table and transform.

Choice: for a team that already keeps Parquet in S3 and wants audit-grade, engine-agnostic branching without copying data, I'd pick lakeFS; DVC is simpler for a small file-based team; Iceberg/Delta time travel is lowest-friction only if they already run a lakehouse, but it's table-format-bound and limited by snapshot expiration/VACUUM.

Reproduction: check out the pinned commit, resolve the pinned dataset version (branch/tag/snapshot or DVC hash), restore the environment and seeds, and re-run. Critically, extend retention so the audited version survives the compliance window: disable premature Delta VACUUM / Iceberg snapshot expiry and S3 lifecycle deletion, and treat old versions as immutable.
